chapterBreakdown.gentle: The complaint sounds familiar: younger people just do not work the way we used to. Chapter 12 asks a better question. `The Boomers All Grown Up` is safest when read as an inheritance chapter, not a stereotype chapter. If Chapter 11 showed how boom-era systems hardened into common sense, this chapter asks what happened when the people shaped by those systems grew up and started running institutions. The frozen anchors help us keep that idea narrow: factory bells, machine rhythm, linear hierarchies, and recognition from above. Those patterns can teach real discipline. They can also teach a narrow picture of what serious work, loyalty, and authority look like. So the chapter is not blaming one age group. It is asking how inherited norms become leadership expectations long after the original conditions have changed. That is the safer reading here overall.
chapterBreakdown.direct: The complaint sounds older than the people receiving it. Chapter 12 is not mainly about boomer personality. It is about boomer adulthood inside institutions. `The Boomers All Grown Up` suggests that the people formed by boom-era systems eventually became the adults running workplaces, promotions, and leadership culture. The frozen anchors from earlier chapters matter here: factory bells, linear hierarchies, and recognition from above describe one serious-work logic. During its rise, that logic may have looked disciplined and successful. Later, the same expectations can feel rigid or misfitted when conditions change. The revised edition adds a chapter and appendix on leading millennials, which is a strong signal that the book sees this friction as leadership-related and generationally visible. The chapter's safest claim is simple. Institutions carry old rules forward through adults who learned those rules early enough that they now feel normal. That is why the clash can look personal.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: The easy move is to call the conflict generational and stop there. Chapter 12 refuses that shortcut. `The Boomers All Grown Up` points at a generation that did not just age. It inherited a work logic and then brought it into power. The frozen anchors keep the claim concrete: bells, hierarchy, and approval from above. Those things can create order. They can also become default signals of seriousness long after the world that rewarded them has changed. That is why the revised-edition focus on leading millennials matters. It suggests the book sees later workplace conflict not as random whining, but as inherited expectations colliding with changed conditions. This chapter is not saying older adults are the problem by nature. It is saying institutions get shaped by the rules their grown-ups learned to trust. That trust can become a blind spot.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The complaint sounds simple: younger workers do not care about work the way older people did. Chapter 12 slows that complaint down. `The Boomers All Grown Up` is safest when read as a chapter about inherited norms rather than fixed personalities. If Chapter 11 argued that boom-era systems hardened into common sense, this chapter asks what happened when the people shaped by those systems became adults and started running workplaces, promotions, and institutions.

The frozen anchors from earlier in the book make that move concrete. We have factory bells, machine rhythm, linear hierarchies, and recognition from above. Those are not only organizational details. They are signals about what serious work looks like. They can teach discipline, patience, and order. But they can also train people to trust status signals that later become too narrow for changed conditions.

That is the chapter's safest mechanism. A generation does not only inherit advantages or disadvantages. It inherits definitions. What counts as loyalty? What counts as commitment? What counts as leadership presence? If those definitions are learned early, they stop feeling historical and start feeling obvious. Adults then carry them into authority and reproduce them through hiring, promotion, praise, and criticism.

The revised 2017 paperback gives one more careful clue. It adds an expanded chapter and appendix on leading millennials. That does not tell us exactly what Chapter 12 says, but it confirms that the book treats workplace friction as both generationally visible and leadership-relevant. The safest conclusion is that the chapter is not inviting lazy boomer-versus-millennial combat. It is asking why younger people entering institutions built around older expectations may experience those expectations as misfit instead of maturity.

The hard limit matters. Not every boomer leader thinks the same way, and not every younger worker wants the same thing. The chapter is stronger than stereotype and narrower than sociology. It says leadership habits can outlive the world that trained them. A generation can carry real strengths forward, like discipline or clarity, while also carrying blind spots that become easier to see only after conditions change. That is why generational conflict is often really institutional inheritance showing itself in human form.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The argument sounds personal until you ask who taught the rules. Chapter 12 takes the boom-and-bust argument and gives it a human carrier. `The Boomers All Grown Up` suggests that earlier work systems did not simply leave behind structures. They also shaped adults who later rose into authority and turned those inherited assumptions into leadership culture. The chapter is strongest when read that way and weakest when reduced to simple age complaint.

The frozen anchors support that narrower reading. Factory bells and machine rhythm describe a work logic built around timing, control, and visible discipline. Linear hierarchies and recognition from above describe a status logic built around approval, rank, and upward orientation. Those patterns may have helped people succeed in the world that rewarded them. The problem is not that they were fake. The problem is that people can mistake what trained them for what is always true.

That is why the title matters. The boomers are all grown up not just because the generation is older, but because it now occupies the institutions where assumptions become expectations. What felt like responsible adulthood in one era becomes promotion criteria in the next. What once looked like loyalty becomes the standard for commitment. What once looked like seriousness becomes the benchmark younger workers are judged against.

The revised edition's added material on leading millennials gives the chapter another narrow support. It shows that the book sees the workplace conflict as persistent enough to warrant explicit leadership attention. That is a signal to read Chapter 12 as an inheritance problem. Older adults shaped by one set of status cues are leading younger adults formed under different conditions. The friction is real, but the book's likely target is not youth or age itself. It is the institution that keeps treating inherited expectations as timeless wisdom.

The chapter only stays honest if it rejects caricature. Not all boomers are rigid. Not all younger workers are restless. A generation is mixed. But institutions are still shaped by what their leaders learned to admire, fear, and reward. That is the real distinction. Generational labels matter here only because they point to different formative conditions. The chapter is ultimately about leadership norms that survived long enough to become invisible. Once that happens, adults can carry yesterday's signals of success into workplaces that now need trust, flexibility, and more human-scale judgment than those signals were built to provide.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The lazy reading says this chapter is about older people versus younger people. The sharper reading is harsher than that. `The Boomers All Grown Up` says institutions are being run by adults who learned their work instincts inside an older success logic and now mistake those instincts for reality itself. That is why Chapter 12 matters.

The frozen anchors keep the claim disciplined. Factory bells, machine rhythm, linear hierarchies, and recognition from above describe a world where seriousness is legible through order, timing, and approval from the top. Those signals can train real strengths. They can also harden into a leadership style that keeps treating older status cues like moral truth long after conditions change.

That is the core mechanism. A generation carries norms forward by turning its training into standards. The adults who rise inside a system do not just inherit jobs. They inherit definitions of loyalty, authority, and good work. Then they encode those definitions into meetings, promotions, criticism, and culture. By the time younger workers push back, leadership often hears attitude instead of mismatch because the institution has forgotten that its own rules were historically produced.

The revised-edition emphasis on leading millennials sharpens the point without giving license for stereotype. It confirms that the book sees leadership friction showing up across generations. The safest conclusion is not that one cohort is virtuous and the other decadent. It is that inherited expectations from one formative world are colliding with people entering under another.

This chapter gets stronger when it keeps one boundary hard. Not every boomer leader is trapped in old assumptions. Not every younger worker is right to resist them. The book is not doing demographic astrology. It is doing institutional diagnosis. The grown-ups matter because they are the carriers. They move old rules into new environments and then call the rules normal adulthood. That is how leadership cultures become outdated without realizing it.

So the accusation is not really against age. It is against uninspected inheritance. If adults keep promoting the signals they were trained to trust, institutions can become museums of yesterday's seriousness while still demanding loyalty from people living in different conditions. That is why the chapter belongs right before `Abstraction Kills`. Once leadership is inherited rather than examined, distance from actual human reality gets easier to scale. The gap stops looking like a problem and starts looking like professionalism. The institution starts mistaking its own age for proof. That is when stale adulthood turns into policy.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The complaint lands like common sense: younger people no longer work the way serious adults should. Chapter 12 asks whether that common sense is actually inherited training. `The Boomers All Grown Up` is safest when read as a chapter about adults carrying forward a formative system, not as a verdict on every member of a generation. If Chapter 11 traced the rise of norms during the boom years, this chapter asks what happened once the people shaped by those norms reached authority and started turning them into culture.

That shift matters because systems survive through human carriers. Factory bells, machine rhythm, linear hierarchies, and recognition from above are not only structures. They are lessons. They teach what discipline looks like, how seriousness is displayed, where approval comes from, and what kind of loyalty gets rewarded. People who grow up inside those signals can absorb them so deeply that the signals stop feeling historical and start feeling morally obvious.

That is the chapter's core mechanism. The boomers are all grown up not simply because the generation got older, but because adulthood means occupying the offices where private formation becomes public expectation. What was once personal training becomes promotion logic. What was once adaptation becomes standard. What once worked under one set of conditions becomes the benchmark used to judge people formed under another.

The revised 2017 edition gives the chapter one more narrow support. It adds an expanded chapter and appendix on leading millennials. That does not license broad social theory, but it does confirm that the book understands workplace friction as visible across generations and relevant to leadership. The safest inference is that Chapter 12 is less interested in blaming a cohort than in showing how inherited norms collide with younger workers entering institutions built around older signals of loyalty, patience, status, and seriousness.

This is why stereotype is the enemy of the chapter. If you say all boomers are rigid, you lose the mechanism. If you say all younger workers are simply different, you lose it again. The chapter works only if it preserves mixed reality. A generation can inherit real strengths from its formative system, like endurance, clarity, and discipline. It can also inherit blind spots, like overtrust in hierarchy or an overly narrow sense of commitment. The problem is not age essence. The problem is uninspected inheritance becoming institutional authority.

That makes the chapter sharper than ordinary generational commentary. It says adults can carry yesterday's seriousness into today's workplaces and mistake it for timeless truth. Once that happens, leadership begins rewarding familiarity rather than fit. Younger people are judged against signals they did not help choose. Older adults defend rules they no longer experience as optional. The conflict then looks like personality when it is really history embodied. The hard limit still matters: no generation explains everything, and the chapter is not a full sociology of work. But it does insist that institutions are historical because their leaders are historical. They bring their formation into power, and that power can keep old rules alive long after the world that trained them has changed. That is the bridge to abstraction, where distance from lived human reality stops looking inherited and starts looking neutral.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
The room sounds generational until you notice whose rules are speaking. Chapter 12 takes the boom-era system and puts it inside an adult body. `The Boomers All Grown Up` is not mainly saying older people are the problem. It is saying institutions are being run by adults shaped inside older work norms and that those norms have become hard to distinguish from common sense. The chapter matters because leadership culture is not only built out of structures. It is built out of what the people in charge learned early enough to stop questioning.

The frozen anchors give that claim a concrete base. Factory bells and machine rhythm describe a world where discipline is legible through timing, repetition, and order. Linear hierarchies and recognition from above describe a world where seriousness and success are legible through rank and approval. Those lessons may have rewarded real competence in the conditions that produced them. The chapter does not need to deny that. It only needs to show how adults can turn rewarded adaptation into permanent expectation.

That is the central mechanism. A generation carries system logic forward by converting its own training into standards for everyone else. Once the boomers are grown up, what they learned to respect can become promotion criteria, management tone, and culture. That is why later workplace conflict can look generational on the surface while being institutional underneath. People entering under different conditions are often judged against inherited signals of loyalty, patience, face time, and seriousness that older adults no longer experience as historically contingent.

The revised-edition emphasis on leading millennials makes that reading stronger. It shows the book sees later workplace friction as real enough to warrant explicit leadership attention. The safe conclusion is not that millennials are right or boomers are wrong. It is that inherited leadership norms from one world are colliding with workers formed in another. The institution experiences that collision as attitude, entitlement, or softness because it keeps treating its own rules as natural adulthood rather than trained adulthood.

That is the chapter's hard edge. Stereotype is too weak for what it is trying to say. Boomers are mixed. Younger workers are mixed. But leaders still transmit norms. They reward what they trust, and they trust what made sense in their own formation unless they examine it. That means a generation can carry forward both strengths and distortions at once. Discipline can survive. So can blind loyalty to hierarchy. Seriousness can survive. So can an overreliance on approval from above.

The chapter only works if it keeps both truths live. Some inherited norms deserve preservation. Others need inspection because the conditions that once made them sensible have changed. Without that distinction, institutions become historical by accident. They keep enforcing yesterday's adulthood on today's people and then misread the friction as moral decline. That is why the chapter belongs here. It turns generational complaint into a leadership diagnosis. The adults in charge are not merely older. They are carriers of a formative system, and once their inherited rules start feeling neutral, abstraction is waiting nearby. The distance from lived human reality becomes easier to defend when it has already been normalized as maturity.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The lazy argument says the workplace is a fight between older people and younger people. Chapter 12 makes a harder accusation. `The Boomers All Grown Up` says institutions are being governed by adults who turned their own formative work signals into standards and then forgot those standards were inherited. That is more serious than stereotype because it explains how history survives inside authority.

The frozen anchors keep the chapter from turning into a rant. Factory bells, machine rhythm, linear hierarchies, and recognition from above describe one older seriousness model. It rewards order, visibility, patience, rank, and upward-facing approval. That model can produce real strengths. It can also train leaders to confuse those strengths with the full definition of commitment, loyalty, and professionalism.

That is the chapter's mechanism. Grown-ups do not just run institutions. They encode their training into them. What once helped them succeed becomes the thing they praise. What once felt responsible becomes the thing they demand. By the time younger workers push against those expectations, leadership often hears weakness instead of mismatch because leadership no longer remembers that its own signals were built under conditions that are no longer universal.

The revised-edition focus on leading millennials sharpens that point. It confirms that the book sees generational friction as a real leadership problem, not a side topic. The cleanest reading is that older adults are carrying inherited norms into workplaces now populated by people formed under different incentives, risks, and expectations. The conflict looks personal because institutions are good at hiding their own history inside words like mature, professional, loyal, and committed.

This chapter gets teeth when it refuses both nostalgia and stereotype. Not every boomer leader is rigid. Not every younger worker is insightful. But that is not the real question anyway. The real question is what kind of adulthood leadership keeps rewarding. If seriousness is still measured through signals inherited from an older work world, then younger people are being judged against a culture that mistakes history for truth. That is why the chapter is stronger than age commentary. It is about norm transfer through power.

The hard limit stays hard. Some inherited norms deserve respect because they carry real discipline, clarity, and endurance. Others survive past their usefulness and become defensive habits dressed up as wisdom. If leaders never separate those two, institutions become museums of the grown-ups who run them. They keep demanding loyalty to signals that no longer fit the people below them and then call the resulting friction generational decline. That is not insight. It is historical amnesia with authority attached. Once that amnesia hardens, abstraction is next. Leadership gets farther from lived reality while still sounding perfectly adult, perfectly serious, and perfectly wrong about why the conflict is happening. It also keeps mistaking old prestige for relevance. That leaves newer workers inside standards nobody re-earned. Soon the standards themselves start sounding objective enough. That is when leadership stops hearing real people clearly.

examples.title: The Retention Problem That Looked Like Attitude Until the Rules Were Named

scenario.gentle: Nora hears senior leaders complain that younger employees leave too quickly and do not respect the culture. When she studies the pattern, she sees that promotion still depends heavily on face time, patience for unclear feedback, and approval from a few senior people.
scenario.direct: The leadership team is calling the issue generational softness. Nora can see that the organization is still rewarding older signals of seriousness and then acting surprised when newer hires disengage.
scenario.competitive: The easy verdict is that the younger staff are flaky. Nora has to decide whether to defend that story or expose the inherited rules behind it.

whatToDo.gentle: She should name the promotion signals openly and ask whether they still measure the kind of contribution the organization actually needs.
whatToDo.direct: Audit the inherited standards before diagnosing the people failing under them.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop calling it attitude until you have proved the rules are not outdated.

whyItMatters.gentle: This is Chapter 12 in practice: older expectations can keep running long after their context changes.
whyItMatters.direct: Nora separates cohort stereotype from institutional inheritance.
whyItMatters.competitive: If she skips that audit, the company keeps protecting its past by blaming the newest people.

examples.title: The Lab Team That Inherited Seniority More Than Leadership

scenario.gentle: After a rough semester, Trent reviews why newer students stopped contributing in the lab team. The postmortem shows that older members controlled decisions almost automatically because that was the tradition they inherited from prior team leads.
scenario.direct: The team blamed younger students for low initiative. The postmortem shows they were entering a culture where authority and respect had already been defined by age and waiting time.
scenario.competitive: The lab thought it had a motivation problem. It had an inherited adulthood script.

whatToDo.gentle: Trent should keep useful structure while reopening real voice and responsibility earlier in the team's life.
whatToDo.direct: Separate disciplined mentorship from automatic seniority and rebuild the process so contribution is not mistaken for age rank.
whatToDo.competitive: Break the old script before the next class mistakes obedience for leadership.

whyItMatters.gentle: This shows how institutional habits get carried forward even when nobody re-chooses them.
whyItMatters.direct: The chapter's point is that people inherit standards before they consciously defend them.
whyItMatters.competitive: If Trent only blames the newest students, he turns inheritance into character judgment.

whyItMatters.direct: Imani's dilemma is about separating durable standards from inherited gatekeeping.
whyItMatters.competitive: If she keeps the trap, she teaches the next class to worship the signal instead of the substance.

examples.title: Before and After Someone Realized the Rule Was Older Than the Problem

scenario.gentle: Before, Lucas assumed the oldest family members were simply tougher and the younger ones were simply less committed. After a series of conversations, he realized the family had inherited a narrow rule about what visible responsibility looked like and had been using it to judge everyone for years.
scenario.direct: The before state is generational blame. The after state begins when Lucas sees that the conflict is being driven by an inherited standard that nobody has examined recently.
scenario.competitive: Before, Lucas called it a values gap. After, he saw an old script still grading new people.

whatToDo.gentle: He should ask what the rule was protecting, then decide which part of it still deserves loyalty and which part has become misfit.
whatToDo.direct: Audit the inherited expectation before making more moral judgments about the people under it.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop calling the younger people weak until you have tested whether the standard itself is stale.

whyItMatters.gentle: This shows how Chapter 12 reframes age conflict as inherited expectation conflict.
whyItMatters.direct: Lucas moves from blaming personalities to examining the history inside the standard.
whyItMatters.competitive: Once the rule gets exposed as inheritance, the whole moral story changes.

questions.prompt: What is the safest reading of `The Boomers All Grown Up`?
choices: A stereotype about older people being difficult
A chapter about adults carrying inherited work norms into leadership
A claim that young workers are always right

explanation.gentle: The chapter is strongest when read as an inheritance story, not a personality attack.
explanation.direct: It asks what happened when people shaped by older systems reached authority.
explanation.competitive: The title points at norm transfer through power, not age-war theater.

questions.prompt: Why does Chapter 12 follow `The Boom Before the Bust` so naturally?
choices: Because it abandons history and talks only about feelings
Because it moves from inherited systems to the adults who carried those systems forward
Because it proves all booms are caused by one generation

explanation.gentle: Chapter 11 asks what norms were built. Chapter 12 asks who embodied them.
explanation.direct: The sequence moves from system inheritance to human inheritance.
explanation.competitive: First the rules harden, then the grown-ups enforce them.

questions.prompt: How do factory bells, hierarchy, and recognition from above function in this chapter?
choices: As proof that old workers were morally superior
As signals of an older work logic that people could inherit as normal
As evidence that all structure should disappear

explanation.gentle: They anchor the chapter in concrete norms about seriousness and authority.
explanation.direct: The chapter uses them as training signals that later become leadership expectations.
explanation.competitive: Old success cues become later judgment cues.

questions.prompt: Nora sees that promotions still reward face time and senior approval, then notices younger staff leaving. What chapter move is she making?
choices: She is separating inherited standards from generational stereotype
She is proving that younger people dislike work
She is ignoring leadership responsibility

explanation.gentle: She is checking the institution's inherited rules before blaming a cohort.
explanation.direct: This is Chapter 12 applied: audit the standard before diagnosing the people under it.
explanation.competitive: Nora refuses to let the old script hide behind a complaint about youth.

questions.prompt: Why does the 2017 edition's added material on leading millennials matter here?
choices: It proves Chapter 12 is entirely about millennials
It confirms that the book treats workplace generational friction as leadership-relevant
It means the earlier chapters no longer matter

explanation.gentle: The edition update is a clue that this cross-generational issue matters to the book.
explanation.direct: It strengthens the chapter's institutional-friction reading without proving broad cohort theory.
explanation.competitive: Use it as support for the collision, not as a license to stereotype.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's core mechanism for how generations shape institutions?
choices: Adults encode what formed them into standards for other people
Every generation naturally rejects all previous norms
Institutions ignore the people who run them

explanation.gentle: People carry their early training into authority and make it feel normal.
explanation.direct: This chapter is about leaders converting formative signals into promotion logic and culture.
explanation.competitive: Grown-ups turn their own training into the rulebook.

questions.prompt: What hard limit keeps Chapter 12 honest?
choices: No generation is uniform, and the chapter rejects stereotype even while tracing influence
Generations do not matter at all
Older norms are always wrong

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps history without collapsing into caricature.
explanation.direct: It preserves mixed strengths and blind spots instead of assigning moral essence by age.
explanation.competitive: This is norm transfer, not demographic astrology.

questions.prompt: Which situation best fits Chapter 12's argument?
choices: A leader assumes younger employees lack loyalty without examining whether the loyalty test itself is inherited
A worker learns a new tool quickly
A team changes its schedule after a storm

explanation.gentle: The chapter asks us to inspect the inherited standard, not just the person being judged.
explanation.direct: Leadership often mistakes historically trained expectations for timeless maturity.
explanation.competitive: The old script stays protected until someone audits the test itself.

questions.prompt: What would Chapter 12 most likely reject as too simplistic?
choices: Older adults carry some real strengths and some blind spots from the systems that formed them
Boomers bad, millennials good
Institutions preserve norms through leaders

explanation.gentle: The chapter specifically resists turning generations into moral cartoons.
explanation.direct: It wants institutional diagnosis, not easy cohort warfare.
explanation.competitive: Cheap age blame misses the mechanism completely.

questions.prompt: Why does this chapter naturally lead into `Abstraction Kills`?
choices: Because once inherited authority feels neutral, distance from real people becomes easier to scale
Because the book is leaving institutions behind
Because generations stop mattering after Chapter 12

explanation.gentle: If old rules are carried into power unquestioned, they can drift away from lived reality.
explanation.direct: The next step after inherited norms is the distance those norms can create from actual human consequences.
explanation.competitive: Once history starts sounding neutral, abstraction is waiting.

coreSkill.gentle: Practice separating inherited work expectations from timeless truth.
coreSkill.direct: Build the habit of auditing where your leadership standards came from before enforcing them on others.
coreSkill.competitive: Train yourself to spot when you are promoting your formation instead of reality.

ifThenPlans.context: you feel a generational complaint forming

plan.gentle: If I start blaming a generation, then I will ask what inherited rule or expectation may be underneath the conflict.
plan.direct: If the issue looks generational, then I will inspect the standard before diagnosing the cohort.
plan.competitive: If I am about to say 'young people,' then I will audit the rule first.

ifThenPlans.context: a leadership norm feels obviously mature

plan.gentle: If an expectation feels natural and serious, then I will ask when and where I learned to trust it.
plan.direct: If a standard feels timeless, then I will test whether it is actually inherited context.
plan.competitive: If a rule feels sacred, then I will assume it needs history checked.

ifThenPlans.context: younger people resist an established signal

plan.gentle: If newer workers resist a long-standing expectation, then I will ask whether the expectation still measures what I think it measures.
plan.direct: If there is friction around loyalty, patience, or seriousness, then I will test the inherited signal instead of only the people under it.
plan.competitive: If the younger group pushes back, then I will prove the old signal still deserves power before defending it.

twentyFourHourChallenge.gentle: Within the next day, choose one workplace or family expectation that feels normal and write down what formative world may have taught it to you.
twentyFourHourChallenge.direct: Run a 24-hour inheritance audit: pick one leadership standard, trace its likely origin, and decide whether it is a durable value or an outdated signal.
twentyFourHourChallenge.competitive: In the next day, catch one rule you call mature and decide whether it is wisdom or just old training with authority.

weeklyPractice.gentle: Each week, review one conflict and ask whether an inherited expectation is hiding under the surface.
weeklyPractice.direct: Once a week, inspect one leadership norm for what it preserves, what it distorts, and who it now misreads.
weeklyPractice.competitive: Every week, find one place where your institution is rewarding old signals as if they were timeless truth.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: Chapter 12 says institutions carry old work norms forward through the adults shaped by them, which is why generational conflict often hides inherited expectations about authority, loyalty, and seriousness.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: This chapter is about historical training in power: leaders often enforce standards that feel timeless only because they were learned early and rewarded for long enough to become invisible.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: The real issue is not age by itself. It is grown-up authority still rewarding inherited signals as if they were reality.
